symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots on leaf surfaces
Yellowing and premature defoliation of infected leaves
Scabby, dark, corky lesions on developing fruit
causes: Fungal pathogen Venturia inaequalis
Prolonged leaf wetness (>9 hours) with cool to moderate temperatures (13°C - 24°C)
Overwintering fungal spores in fallen infected leaf litter
treatment: Prune affected twigs and rake up all fallen leaves beneath canopy
Apply protective or systemic fungicide in accordance with regional agricultural extension recommendations
Bio-fungicide applications containing Bacillus subtilis can help suppress early spore germination
prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple cultivars when establishing new orchards
Maintain open canopy pruning to promote rapid leaf drying
Apply clean mulch around tree bases to isolate soil-borne spores
agricultural_advice: Scout orchard blocks weekly during springtime bud break and petal fall.
Monitor weather forecasts for continuous rainy spells and treat ahead of long wetting events.

symptoms: Small purple flecks expanding into frog-eye leaf spots with brown centers
Firm brown rotting lesions on fruit turning coal-black and mummified
Sunken reddish-brown cankers on branches and limbs
causes: Fungal pathogen Botryosphaeria obtusa
Warm, humid conditions with splashing rain disseminating spores
Dead wood, mummified fruit, and pruning wounds acting as spore reservoirs
treatment: Prune out dead branches, twigs, and cankers at least 15 cm below infected tissue
Remove and safely burn or bury all mummified fruits from previous seasons
Apply approved broad-spectrum fungicide sprays from petal fall through midsummer
prevention: Avoid bark injuries and maintain balanced tree nutrition to resist canker entry
Sanitize pruning shears between cuts using 70% alcohol or dilute bleach solution
Ensure proper air circulation through regular seasonal pruning
agricultural_advice: Regularly sanitize orchard floors and remove all mummified apples hanging in the winter canopy.

symptoms: Bright orange-yellow circular spots on upper leaf surfaces
Tiny black pycnidia forming in the center of yellow spots
Tubular spore-bearing structures (aecia) protruding on the underside of leaves
causes: Fungal pathogen Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae
Alternating life cycle between apple trees and nearby Eastern Red Cedar / Juniper hosts
Windborne spores traveling during wet spring conditions
treatment: Apply appropriate protective fungicide sprays from pink bud stage until aecia maturation
Remove nearby wild red cedar trees or galls within 1–2 km of commercial apple blocks if feasible
prevention: Select rust-resistant apple varieties (e.g., Liberty, Enterprise, Redfree)
Inspect adjacent landscaping and windbreaks for cedar galls that release spores after warm rain
agricultural_advice: Rust infection risk peaks during bloom through early fruit set when cedar galls produce gelatinous spore horns.

symptoms: No foliar lesions, chlorosis, or necrotic margins detected
Uniform green coloration with smooth leaf epidermis and intact venation
causes: Optimal cultivation conditions, balanced fertilization, and effective pest management
treatment: No curative disease intervention required
Maintain regular crop monitoring and preventative scouting
prevention: Continue standard irrigation and balanced fertilization programs
Keep orchard floor clean of diseased debris
agricultural_advice: Maintain periodic routine scouting every 7–10 days to confirm continued disease-free status.

symptoms: Vibrant green leaves with no necrotic spots, chlorosis, or leaf curl
Normal shoot elongation and healthy vegetative vigor
causes: Optimal soil pH (4.5–5.5), adequate moisture, and robust root health
treatment: No treatment necessary
prevention: Maintain acidic soil conditions with pine bark mulch or sulfur amendments
Ensure drip irrigation prevents drought stress
agricultural_advice: Check soil moisture and pH regularly to support continued vigorous vegetative growth.

symptoms: White powdery fungal patches on young leaves and terminal shoot tips
Upward curling, distortion, and blistering of young leaves
Stunted shoot growth and possible fruit russeting
causes: Fungal pathogen Podosphaera clandestina
Warm days (20°C - 27°C) with high relative humidity and shaded canopies
Overcrowded branch architecture preventing airflow
treatment: Prune heavily infected terminal shoot tips to decrease local inoculum
Apply potassium bicarbonate, horticultural oils, or sulfur-based fungicides as recommended locally
Alternate fungicide chemistries to prevent resistance development
prevention: Prune trees to open up interior light and facilitate rapid air movement
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization which promotes susceptible lush tender growth
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation
agricultural_advice: Begin monitoring young leaf flushes during late spring and apply protective sprays before extensive leaf curling occurs.

symptoms: Clean, unblemished green leaves without powdery coatings or spots
causes: Well-managed orchard practices with balanced moisture and nutrition
treatment: No treatment required
prevention: Maintain preventative seasonal pest and disease scouting
agricultural_advice: Maintain good orchard hygiene and monitor for insect vectors.

symptoms: Narrow rectangular lesions parallel to leaf veins, tan to gray in color
Lesions restricted by parallel leaf veins giving distinct blocky appearance
Blighting of entire leaves and premature stalk lodging
causes: Fungal pathogen Cercospora zeae-maydis
Warm, humid weather with prolonged dew (>12 hours) and frequent fog
Continuous no-till corn cropping where infected residue remains on the soil surface
treatment: Apply labeled foliar fungicides between tasseling (VT) and early silking (R1) if threshold is reached
Target susceptible hybrids under high disease pressure
prevention: Select corn hybrids with high genetic tolerance to Gray Leaf Spot
Rotate crops away from corn for at least one season to allow residue decomposition
Use conventional tillage in high-risk continuous-corn fields where appropriate
agricultural_advice: Scout the lower third of corn plants prior to tasseling. Treat if lesions appear on the third leaf below the ear leaf or higher on susceptible hybrids.

symptoms: Oval to elongate cinnamon-brown pustules scattered across both upper and lower leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture the leaf epidermis, releasing powdery rust-colored urediniospores
Severe infections cause yellowing and premature leaf death
causes: Fungal pathogen Puccinia sorghi
Cool to moderate temperatures (16°C - 25°C) combined with high relative humidity (>95%)
Windborne spores transported over long distances from southern overwintering zones
treatment: Foliar fungicides may be warranted on high-value sweet corn or seed corn if rust appears early
In commercial field corn, treatment is rarely economical unless susceptible hybrids are infected before silking
prevention: Plant corn hybrids possessing resistant genes (e.g., Rp gene family)
Plant early in the season to mature the crop before peak regional spore arrival
agricultural_advice: Distinguish from Southern Rust (which has smaller, orange pustules primarily on the upper leaf surface) by noting pustules on both leaf sides.

symptoms: Long, elliptical, cigar-shaped grayish-green to tan lesions (2.5 to 15 cm long)
Dark olive sporulation visible within lesions under humid conditions
Lesions coalesce, blighting large areas of the canopy
causes: Fungal pathogen Exserohilum turcicum
Moderate temperatures (18°C - 27°C) accompanied by extended periods of leaf wetness (6–18 hours)
Survival in infected corn debris on the soil surface
treatment: Apply approved foliar fungicides between V12 and R1 if weather favors disease and hybrid is susceptible
Ensure thorough canopy coverage with proper spray pressure
prevention: Plant hybrids carrying race-specific resistance genes (Ht genes) or robust quantitative resistance
Practice two-year crop rotation out of corn
Incorporate crop residue after harvest to accelerate decomposition
agricultural_advice: Assess ear leaf and adjacent leaves during pollination; severe blighting during grain fill can reduce yield by 30–50%.

symptoms: Broad, vibrant green leaves free of rectangular lesions, rust pustules, or blights
Normal leaf elongation and vigorous stalk development
causes: Adequate soil fertility, balanced nitrogen availability, and minimal moisture stress
treatment: No curative action required
prevention: Continue balanced fertility management and integrated pest scouting
agricultural_advice: Scout during critical growth stages (V6, VT/R1) to maintain proactive surveillance.

symptoms: Small circular reddish-brown leaf spots with dark borders and tiny black fruiting bodies
Berries turn pale, then brown, shriveling into hard, black, mummified prunes
Black oval lesions on canes, petioles, and tendrils
causes: Fungal pathogen Guignardia bidwellii
Warm (21°C - 27°C), wet weather with prolonged rainfall and dew
Overwintered mummified berries left on the vine or on the vineyard floor
treatment: Apply preventative fungicides from early shoot growth through 4–5 weeks post-bloom
Prune out infected canes and manually remove all clinging mummified clusters
prevention: Canopy management: shoot positioning and leaf removal around fruit clusters to maximize air movement
Destroy or bury mummified berries during winter dormancy
agricultural_advice: Critical infection control window is from immediate pre-bloom through 4 weeks post-bloom.

symptoms: Tiger-stripe pattern of interveinal chlorosis and necrosis on mature leaves
Dark purple-brown spotting on fruit skin ('measles')
Internal trunk wood shows brown or black vascular streaking and spongy white rot
causes: Complex of wood-rotting fungal pathogens including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Fomitiporia mediterranea
Infection entering through large pruning wounds during wet winter conditions
treatment: No direct chemical cure exists for infected vine trunks
Prune out infected cordons back to clean white wood and train a renewal sucker
Severely affected non-productive vines should be uprooted and replaced
prevention: Delayed pruning: prune vines late in dormancy when wounds heal more rapidly
Paint large pruning wounds with wound sealants or protective biocontrol agents
Avoid making large flush cuts close to trunk trunks
agricultural_advice: Mark symptomatic vines in the summer so they can be addressed or retrained during winter pruning.

symptoms: Irregular brown necrotic lesions on leaves, often surrounded by yellow chlorotic margins
Lesions coalesce late in the season leading to early defoliation and delayed berry ripening
causes: Fungal pathogen Pseudocercospora cladosporioides (Isariopsis clavispora)
High humidity, frequent summer rain, and dense shaded vine canopies
treatment: Apply standard grape foliar protectant fungicides during mid-to-late season
Remove severely blighted foliage post-harvest
prevention: Maintain open canopy architecture via summer leaf pulling and shoot hedging
Improve air drainage across vineyard rows
agricultural_advice: Keep foliage protected through post-harvest to preserve sugar reserves for winter hardiness.

symptoms: Clean, fully expanded green leaves with intact margins and healthy fruit clusters
causes: Balanced canopy management, adequate trellis exposure, and timely pest scouting
treatment: No treatment required
prevention: Continue seasonal canopy management and cluster zone leaf removal
agricultural_advice: Maintain regular vineyard scouting every week during fruit enlargement and veraison.

symptoms: Asymmetric blotchy mottling of leaf blades with yellowing crossing major veins
Yellow shoots (shoots turning golden while remainder of canopy is green)
Small, lopsided, bitter fruit that stays green at the blossom end ('greening')
causes: Bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus
Vectored by the Asian Citrus Psyllid (Diaphorina citri)
Graft transmission from infected budwood
treatment: There is currently no cure for trees infected with Huanglongbing
Manage psyllid vector populations aggressively using coordinated area-wide spray programs
Remove confirmed infected trees to eliminate inoculum reservoirs for surrounding groves
Provide foliar micronutrient therapies to maintain productivity of mildly affected trees
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free nursery stock grown in enclosed screenhouses
Conduct continuous psyllid trapping and chemical vector control
Comply with citrus quarantine regulations regarding transport of plant material
agricultural_advice: Inspect tree flushes for characteristic blotchy mottle (asymmetrical yellowing across veins) and scout for nymph and adult psyllids.

symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked spots on leaves turning purple to dark brown
Infected leaf centers drop out leaving a 'shot-hole' appearance
Cracking, gumming, and pitted lesions on developing peach fruit
causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni
Wind-driven rain, blowing sand, and warm humid weather (24°C - 30°C)
Sandy soils and abrasive conditions that cause micro-wounds on leaf and fruit tissue
treatment: Apply copper sprays during dormancy and early season according to label safety limits
Oxytetracycline sprays may be applied during bloom through petal fall under high disease pressure
Avoid excessive copper doses during active leafing to prevent phytotoxicity
prevention: Select resistant peach varieties suited to your growing area
Establish windbreaks to reduce windblown sand and mechanical wounding
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization that creates succulent, susceptible growth
agricultural_advice: Dormant copper sprays significantly reduce bacterial overwintering populations in branch twigs.

symptoms: Vibrant green lanceolate leaves with smooth margins and no shot-hole spotting
causes: Optimal orchard site with good air drainage and balanced seasonal management
treatment: No treatment required
prevention: Maintain preventative dormant sprays and routine insect scouting
agricultural_advice: Continue monitoring for peach tree borer and fungal issues during warm summer spells.

symptoms: Small, water-soaked, circular to irregular lesions on leaves with yellow halos
Lesions turn dark brown to black and can cause substantial premature defoliation
Small, blister-like raised scabs on green bell peppers
causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas euvesicatoria / Xanthomonas perforans
Warm temperatures (24°C - 30°C) with high humidity, heavy rain, and overhead sprinkler splash
Contaminated seed lots and infected transplant seedlings
treatment: Apply copper-based bactericides combined with mancozeb for improved efficacy
Use biologicals such as Bacillus amyloliquefaciens or bacteriophage treatments where available
Promptly remove severely infected plants in small-scale plantings
prevention: Use certified disease-free, hot-water-treated seeds and inspected healthy transplants
Select bell pepper hybrids bred with race-specific bacterial spot resistance (Xcv 1–10)
Strictly avoid overhead irrigation; utilize drip irrigation systems
agricultural_advice: Avoid working in pepper fields when foliage is wet from rain or dew to prevent mechanically spreading bacteria between plants.

symptoms: Glossy, deep-green, uniform leaves without spotting, stunting, or curling
causes: Good soil aeration, balanced calcium and nitrogen levels, and drip irrigation
treatment: No curative action required
prevention: Maintain regular drip irrigation and scout weekly for aphids and bacterial spotting
agricultural_advice: Monitor calcium nutrition to prevent blossom end rot as fruit begins sizing.

symptoms: Circular brown-to-black spots with characteristic concentric rings (target-like pattern)
Yellow chlorotic halos surrounding lesions on older lower foliage
Severe infections cause leaves to dry up, wither, and hang down on the stem
causes: Fungal pathogen Alternaria solani
Alternating wet and dry periods with warm daytime temperatures (24°C - 29°C)
Crop stress from heavy tuber bulking, nitrogen deficiency, or drought
treatment: Apply protectant or systemic fungicides (e.g., chlorothalonil, azoxystrobin) beginning at canopy closure
Ensure uniform coverage of the lower canopy foliage where disease initiates
prevention: Rotate fields away from potatoes, tomatoes, and eggplants for 3 years
Maintain adequate nitrogen and moisture to avoid physiological plant stress during tuber bulking
Destroy and bury volunteer potato plants and harvest culls
agricultural_advice: Disease pressure escalates rapidly as potato vines mature and divert energy into tuber expansion.

symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked lesions turning dark brown to purplish-black
Delicate white fungal-like growth visible on the underside of leaves during high humidity
Rapidly spreading rot affecting stems and producing brown, dry rot inside tubers
causes: Oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans
Cool to moderate temperatures (12°C - 22°C) combined with high relative humidity (>90%) and frequent rain
Infected seed tubers and cull piles acting as early-season primary inoculum sources
treatment: Immediately apply targeted anti-oomycete fungicides upon first regional disease forecast warning
In severe, uncontrollable outbreaks, chemically desiccate foliage to prevent spore washdown into tubers
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free seed potatoes
Eliminate all cull piles and volunteer potato sprouts before the growing season starts
Select potato cultivars with documented late blight resistance
agricultural_advice: Late blight is a community-level threat; report outbreaks immediately to agricultural extension agents to alert neighboring growers.

symptoms: Dark green compound leaves with upright growth habit and no target lesions or water-soaked patches
causes: Certified seed stock, balanced soil fertility, and optimal hilling practices
treatment: No treatment required
prevention: Maintain preventative late blight monitoring using regional weather advisory alerts
agricultural_advice: Hill potatoes adequately to shield developing tubers from sunlight and spore washdown.

symptoms: Bright green serrated leaflets without yellowing, rust, or cane cankers
causes: Well-drained soil, adequate organic matter, and good air circulation
treatment: No treatment required
prevention: Prune out spent floricanes after fruiting to improve canopy ventilation
agricultural_advice: Trellis canes neatly to prevent foliage from touching wet soil.

symptoms: Trifoliate leaves exhibiting uniform green coloration without rust pustules or chlorotic mottling
causes: Effective inoculation, healthy root nodules, and favorable seasonal rainfall
treatment: No treatment required
prevention: Practice standard crop rotation with corn or small grains
agricultural_advice: Scout during R1 to R3 reproductive stages for late-season foliar diseases.

symptoms: White, talcum-powder-like fungal patches on upper and lower leaf surfaces and petioles
Leaves turn yellow, brown, become brittle, and die prematurely
Exposed fruit suffers sunburn and poor sugar accumulation
causes: Fungal pathogens Podosphaera xanthii and Golovinomyces cichoracearum
Warm temperatures (20°C - 28°C), high humidity at night, and dense foliage shade
Does not require liquid free water for spore germination
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (potassium bicarbonate, sulfur, or approved synthetic fungicides) at first sign of powdery patches
Horticultural oils and neem oil products are effective for organic suppression
prevention: Select powdery mildew-resistant squash and pumpkin cultivars
Provide generous plant spacing to maximize air and sunlight penetration
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization
agricultural_advice: Inspect the shaded undersides of older, lower crown leaves where powdery mildew typically initiates.

symptoms: Numerous small, irregular, purple to dark red spots on leaves
Spots enlarge and centers turn dark brown or purple without white centers
Leaves scorch, curl up along edges, and take on a burnt, dried appearance
causes: Fungal pathogen Diplocarpon earlianum
Frequent rain, overhead sprinkler irrigation, and long periods of leaf wetness
Inoculum surviving on infected living leaves through the winter
treatment: Apply labeled fungicides during spring when new leaves emerge and post-harvest renovation
Mow and destroy infected foliage immediately following harvest renovation
prevention: Plant certified disease-free strawberry runners
Space plants properly and use straw mulch to facilitate rapid drying
Convert to drip irrigation to avoid foliar wetting
agricultural_advice: Differentiate from Leaf Spot (which has distinct white-centered spots) by noting solid purple-brown lesions without white centers.

symptoms: Trifoliate leaves with vibrant green luster, uniform serration, and vigorous runner growth
causes: Raised beds, plastic or straw mulching, and optimized drip fertigation
treatment: No treatment required
prevention: Maintain clean straw mulch beneath developing berries
agricultural_advice: Scout crowns and underside of leaves regularly for two-spotted spider mites.

symptoms: Small, dark, greasy, water-soaked spots on leaves (<3 mm)
Spots turn purplish-brown with yellow chlorotic borders
Raised, scab-like, blistered spots on developing green fruit
causes: Bacterial complex Xanthomonas perforans, X. vesicatoria, X. euvesicatoria, and X. gardneri
Warm (24°C - 30°C) rainy weather with wind-driven splash
Infected seed lots and diseased greenhouse transplants
treatment: Apply fixed copper bactericides combined with mancozeb
Incorporate biological controls (Bacillus amyloliquefaciens or bacteriophages) to combat copper-resistant strains
Remove heavily infected individual plants in small gardens
prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seeds and certified disease-free transplants
Sanitize stakes, greenhouse flats, and tools using disinfectant solutions
Employ drip irrigation to eliminate overhead water splash
agricultural_advice: Do not enter tomato fields or prune plants while foliage is wet from rain or morning dew.

symptoms: Dark brown to black necrotic concentric rings (target-board pattern) on older lower leaves
Chlorotic yellow halos developing around enlarging lesions
Premature defoliation exposing green fruit to sunscald
causes: Fungal pathogen Alternaria solani
Warm temperatures (24°C - 29°C) coupled with high humidity or frequent rainfall
Spores splashing from infected soil debris onto lower canopy leaves
treatment: Prune and destroy severely infected lower leaves up to 45 cm from the soil surface
Apply protective fungicides (e.g., copper octanoate, chlorothalonil, or azoxystrobin) according to local recommendations
Bio-fungicides based on Bacillus subtilis can provide effective suppression in organic systems
prevention: Stake and cage tomato vines to keep foliage elevated off the ground
Apply organic mulch around stems to create a physical barrier against soil-splashing spores
Water exclusively via drip irrigation at the base of the plant
agricultural_advice: Scout lower leaves every 3–4 days during warm, humid spells. Prune off initial target spots before disease spreads upward.

symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked pale green lesions turning dark brown to purplish-black
White fuzzy mildew growth on leaf undersides in high humidity
Dark brown greasy firm rot on tomato fruits
causes: Oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans
Cool, damp, foggy, or rainy conditions (15°C - 22°C with >90% humidity)
Spores carried on regional wind currents from infected potatoes or tomatoes
treatment: Apply targeted late blight fungicides immediately upon regional alert notifications
Severely blighted tomato vines should be removed, bagged on-site, and destroyed immediately to prevent local epidemic spread
prevention: Plant late blight-resistant tomato varieties (e.g., Mountain Magic, Defiant, Plum Regal)
Eliminate cull piles and volunteer potatoes near tomato plantings
Maximize airflow and sunlight exposure between plant rows
agricultural_advice: Late blight can destroy an entire field within 7–10 days; act decisively upon the first confirmed local detection.

symptoms: Pale green to yellowish indistinct spots on upper leaf surfaces
Dense, olive-green to brown velvety fungal growth on the corresponding lower leaf surface
Leaves turn yellow, curl, wither, and drop prematurely
causes: Fungal pathogen Passalora fulva (formerly Cladosporium fulvum)
High relative humidity (>85%) and warm temperatures (21°C - 24°C)
Most prevalent in protected greenhouse, high tunnel, or polytunnel production
treatment: Improve greenhouse ventilation: run circulation fans and open side curtains to reduce relative humidity below 85%
Apply approved copper or bio-fungicide sprays to upper and lower leaf surfaces
prevention: Choose leaf mold-resistant tomato hybrids
Prune lower suckers and leaves to enhance air movement through the dense tunnel canopy
Heat and ventilate high tunnels in the evening to prevent nighttime condensation on leaves
agricultural_advice: Maintain active air circulation inside tunnels; leaf mold rarely thrives when relative humidity is kept below 85%.

symptoms: Numerous small (2–3 mm), circular spots with dark brown margins and light gray/tan centers
Tiny black specks (pycnidia) visible inside the center of mature spots
Infection begins on lowest leaves and progresses rapidly upward, causing widespread defoliation
causes: Fungal pathogen Septoria lycopersici
Moderate to warm temperatures (20°C - 26°C) and extended wet weather or heavy dew
Fungal spores overwintering in solanaceous weed hosts and tomato debris
treatment: Prune off affected lower leaves as soon as first spots appear
Apply protective fungicides (chlorothalonil, copper fungicides) on a regular schedule during wet weather
prevention: Mulch heavily under plants to prevent soil and rain splashback
Rotate out of tomatoes, potatoes, and peppers for at least 2–3 years
Keep garden free of horsenettle, groundcherry, and nightshade weeds
agricultural_advice: Distinguish from Early Blight: Septoria spots are smaller, circular with distinct gray centers and black dots, lacking concentric rings.

symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling (tiny speckled dots) across upper leaf surfaces
Delicate silken webbing visible on leaf undersides and terminal shoots
Leaves turn bronze, dry out, and drop prematurely in heavy infestations
causes: Arachnid pest Tetranychus urticae
Hot, dry, and dusty conditions (above 30°C) with low relative humidity
Overuse of broad-spectrum insecticides which eliminate natural beneficial predatory mites
treatment: Spray leaf undersides with strong water jets to knock down mite populations and disrupt webbing
Apply insecticidal soaps, horticultural oils, or neem extract for gentle suppression
Introduce biological predatory mites (e.g., Phytoseiulus persimilis) in enclosed greenhouses
prevention: Keep pathways and surrounding soil moist and dust-free
Avoid broad-spectrum pyrethroid insecticides that trigger mite flare-ups by killing natural enemies
Regularly inspect leaf undersides with a 10x hand lens during hot summer weather
agricultural_advice: Focus scouting on field edges and dusty perimeter rows during midsummer heat waves.

symptoms: Small, pinpoint water-soaked spots expanding into brown circular lesions with subtle concentric rings
Lesions do not conform strictly to leaf veins and cause extensive canopy defoliation
Fruit develops sunken, circular, brown lesions with dark centers
causes: Fungal pathogen Corynespora cassiicola
Warm temperatures (20°C - 30°C) accompanied by high relative humidity and long periods of leaf wetness
treatment: Apply labeled fungicides such as azoxystrobin, chlorothalonil, or copper compounds
Prune lower canopy leaves to promote faster drying
prevention: Ensure wide plant spacing and vertical staking
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer that promotes dense, moist foliage canopies
Practice 3-year crop rotation
agricultural_advice: Target spot often resembles early blight; check fruit lesions and spray early before canopy closure.

symptoms: Marked stunting and erect, bushy growth habit in infected plants
Upward curling and cup-shaped crumpling of leaf margins
Interveinal yellowing (chlorosis) and reduced leaf size
Severe blossom drop with almost complete cessation of fruit set
causes: Begomovirus (Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus)
Transmitted by the Silverleaf Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
Not seedborne or mechanically transmitted through touch
treatment: No chemical cure exists once a plant is infected with the virus
Immediately rogue out (remove and destroy) infected plants to prevent serving as whitefly virus sources
Manage whitefly vectors with insecticidal soaps, systemic insecticides, or reflective silver mulches
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant tomato cultivars (e.g., Tycoon, Charger, Invicta)
Use fine mesh insect netting (50-mesh) on nursery seedlings and greenhouse openings
Install yellow sticky cards to detect early whitefly arrivals
agricultural_advice: Early-season virus protection is essential; plants infected before flowering yield virtually no marketable fruit.

symptoms: Mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns on leaves
Leaves may become distorted, blistered, or narrowed into 'shoestring' or 'fern-like' shapes
Stunted growth, internal brown browning of fruit walls, and uneven fruit ripening
causes: Tobamovirus (Tomato Mosaic Virus)
Extremely stable mechanically transmitted virus: spreads via contaminated hands, tools, and tobacco products
Survives for years on dry seed coats and in un-decomposed root debris
treatment: There is no chemical cure for viral plant infections
Carefully pull up and dispose of infected plants without brushing them against healthy neighbors
prevention: Plant certified virus-free seed or resistant tomato varieties (look for 'Tm' or 'ToMV' resistance on seed packets)
Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water after handling tobacco products before touching tomato crops
Disinfect pruning shears and stakes in a 10–20% non-fat dry milk solution or 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP)
agricultural_advice: ToMV is one of the most mechanically durable plant viruses known; prioritize sanitation and tool sterilization.

symptoms: Deep green, well-developed compound leaves with no necrotic spots, yellow halos, or curling
Vigorous stem growth, active blossom formation, and smooth, unblemished fruit development
causes: Balanced soil fertility, drip irrigation, vertical staking, and consistent disease scouting
treatment: No curative action required
prevention: Maintain preventative pruning of bottom leaves to avoid soil splash
Continue regular scouting every 3–5 days
agricultural_advice: Maintain consistent soil moisture to prevent blossom end rot, and keep foliage dry to maintain disease-free vigor.

symptoms: Water-soaked to yellowish translucent stripes along leaf margins
Lesions turn white to grayish with wavy margins along leaf blades
Milky bacterial ooze droplets drying into yellow beads on young leaves
causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae
High humidity (80-100%), warm temperatures (25°C - 34°C), and strong winds or rainstorms
Excessive nitrogen application causing lush vegetative growth
treatment: Drain infected fields temporarily to reduce humidity around root zone
Apply recommended copper-based bactericides or plant antibiotics where registered
Avoid excessive nitrogen top-dressing during disease outbreaks
prevention: Plant resistant rice varieties (e.g., carrying Xa21 or Xa4 resistance genes)
Ensure proper field drainage and balanced N-P-K fertilization
Remove volunteer rice plants and weed hosts along paddy bunds
agricultural_advice: Scout fields closely after tropical storms or wind-driven heavy rains when bacterial entry through leaf wounds is highest.

symptoms: Small, oval to circular reddish-brown to dark brown spots scattered on leaves
Mature lesions have yellow chlorotic halos around dark centers
Severe infections cause foliage blighting and poor grain filling
causes: Fungal pathogen Bipolaris oryzae (Helminthosporium oryzae)
Nutrient-deficient, poorly drained, or silicon-depleted soils
Drought stress or soil potassium deficiency
treatment: Apply foliar potassium and silicon soil amendments to strengthen cell walls
Apply protective fungicides (e.g., mancozeb or edifenphos) at early tillering stage
prevention: Balance soil fertility with adequate potassium, phosphorus, and micronutrients
Use certified clean, fungicide-treated seeds
Maintain continuous optimal flood depth to avoid soil drying
agricultural_advice: Brown spot is often an indicator of soil nutritional deficiency rather than aggressive pathogen pressure alone.

symptoms: Diamond-shaped or spindle-shaped lesions with pointed ends and gray/white centers
Lesions surrounded by reddish-brown borders and chlorotic halos
Lesions coalesce causing entire leaf blades to dry and wither ('blast')
causes: Fungal pathogen Magnaporthe oryzae (Pyricularia oryzae)
High atmospheric humidity (>90%), cool night temperatures (17°C - 22°C), and dew
Excessive nitrogen fertilizer creating soft, susceptible leaf tissue
treatment: Apply systemic blast fungicides (e.g., tricyclazole, isoprothiolane, or azoxystrobin) at first sign of spindle lesions
Increase water level in paddies to suppress spore multiplication
prevention: Plant blast-resistant rice cultivars suited to regional microclimates
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer; split applications evenly across growth stages
Maintain proper seedling density to avoid dense canopy humidity
agricultural_advice: Leaf blast can quickly transition to neck blast during flowering, causing total crop failure if left unmonitored.

symptoms: Vibrant green, upright leaf blades free of spindle spots, brown lesions, or leaf margin blighting
causes: Optimal water level management, balanced N-P-K fertilization, and healthy root systems
treatment: No curative action required
prevention: Maintain consistent water management and split nitrogen top-dressings
agricultural_advice: Scout during tillering and panicle initiation to maintain disease-free canopy development.
